content: Dopamine and serotonin are the primary neurotransmitters involved in the regulation of vomiting, both within the central nervous system and the gastrointestinal tract. The most frequent causes of vomiting include gastroenteritis, migraines, gastroparesis, postoperative nausea, radiationand chemotherapy-induced vomiting, tumors, increased intracranial pressure, hepatitis, cholecystitis, labyrinthitis, alcohol abuse, and pregnancy-related vomiting. The management of nausea and vomiting typically relies on obtaining a thorough medical history and performing a detailed physical examination. In most cases, episodes of vomiting lasting less than 48 hours are triggered by identifiable factors such as infections, viral illnesses, or food poisoning. These cases can often be managed by addressing the underlying cause and providing supportive care. Chronic or unexplained nausea and vomiting can be challenging to treat, as the underlying cause is often unclear and may require specialized diagnostic investigations. Causes of Vomiting Life-Threatening Causes Life-threatening causes of vomiting include: Head injury Bowel obstruction Appendicitis Meningitis Myocardial infarction Brain tumors Pancreatitis Common Causes Common causes of vomiting include: Gastric outlet obstruction Small bowel obstruction Irritable bowel syndrome Pancreatic adenocarcinoma Hepatitis Cholecystitis Pancreatitis Crohn’s disease Gastroparesis Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction Postoperative nausea and vomiting Central nervous system (CNS) causes, such as: Migraines Increased intracranial pressure Malignancy Hemorrhage Infarction Abscess Meningitis Congenital malformations Hydrocephalus Pseudotumor cerebri Seizure disorders Demyelinating disorders Infectious causes, such as: Gastroenteritis Otitis media Pseudotumor cerebri Acute intermittent porphyria Labyrinthine disorders, such as: Motion sickness Labyrinthitis Tumors Meniere’s disease Iatrogenic causes Endocrinological and metabolic causes, such as: Pregnancy Uremia Diabetic ketoacidosis Hyperparathyroidism Hypoparathyroidism Hyperthyroidism Addison’s disease Miscellaneous causes, such as: Cardiac disease Myocardial infarction Congestive heart failure Radiofrequency ablation Starvation Cancer chemotherapy Radiation therapy Cardiovascular medications, including: Digoxin Antiarrhythmics Antihypertensives Beta-blockers Calcium-channel antagonists Antibiotics or antivirals Ethanol abuse Renal infections or renal stones Diagnosis The diagnosis of vomiting involves a systematic approach, often summarized in diagnostic algorithms, to identify the underlying cause. Treatment The treatment of vomiting is guided by algorithms that address the underlying cause and provide supportive care. Recommendations (Dos) Encourage patients to take small, frequent sips of water to prevent dehydration. Advise patients to consume sweet drinks, such as fruit juice, to replace lost sugar, unless these exacerbate nausea. Recommend salty snacks, such as crisps, to help replenish lost sodium. Precautions (Don’ts) Patients with a history of diabetes managed with insulin should consult their physician before administering insulin during episodes of continuous vomiting, as vomiting can significantly alter blood sugar levels.
